claim: APOE-ɛ4 is the greatest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: The greatest genetic risk factor for developing late-onset AD is the apolipoprotein E4 (APOE-ɛ4) allele (Corder et al., 1993; van der Flier et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corder et al., 1993 and van der Flier et al., 2011

claim: APOE consists of 299 amino acids divided into receptor-binding and lipid-binding regions.
source: APOE consists of 299 amino acids divided into receptor-binding and lipid-binding regions and has three isoforms (ɛ2, ɛ3 and ɛ4) that only differ at two of the amino acids (112 and 158), both of which are on the receptor-binding part of the protein.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about APOE protein structure

claim: APOE has three isoforms (ɛ2, ɛ3 and ɛ4) that only differ at two amino acids (112 and 158).
source: APOE consists of 299 amino acids divided into receptor-binding and lipid-binding regions and has three isoforms (ɛ2, ɛ3 and ɛ4) that only differ at two of the amino acids (112 and 158), both of which are on the receptor-binding part of the protein.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about APOE isoforms

claim: APOE has a crucial role in transporting cholesterol and other lipids, both in plasma and in the brain.
source: APOE has a crucial role in transporting cholesterol and other lipids, both in plasma and in the brain, but it is its role in regulating amyloid-β that has received much attention, due to the latter's apparently crucial role in AD (Reinvang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reinvang et al., 2013 and Zhao et al., 2018

claim: APOE-ɛ4 stimulates increased recycling of the amyloid precursor protein (APP), leading to an increase in amyloid-β production compared to APOE-ɛ3.
source: For example, compared to APOE-ɛ3, APOE-ɛ4 stimulates increased recycling of the amyloid precursor protein (APP), hence leading to an increase in amyloid-β production (Ye et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ye et al., 2005

claim: APOE-ɛ4 increases amyloid-β production via modified interactions between APOE-ɛ4 and the LRP1 receptor.
source: This mostly appears to be via modified interactions between APOE-ɛ4 and the LRP1 receptor.
evidence: Based on inference from the preceding discussion of APOE-ɛ4 mechanisms

claim: APOE can bind to amyloid-β to form a complex that promotes clearance via cell internalization.
source: Similarly, it has been shown that APOE can bind to amyloid-β to form a complex that then promotes clearance via cell internalization of this complex (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2018

claim: The APOE-ɛ4-amyloid-β complex is less stable than complexes formed by other APOE isoforms, making it less effective in amyloid clearance.
source: As the APOE-ɛ4-amyloid-β complex is less stable than the other isoforms, this may make it less effective in amyloid clearance.
evidence: Based on inference from the stability properties of the complex

claim: APOE-ɛ4 may interfere with protease-mediated clearance of amyloid-β via downregulation of insulin-degrading-enzyme (IDE).
source: Finally, APOE-ɛ4 may interfere with protease-mediated clearance of amyloid-β via downregulation of, for example, insulin-degrading-enzyme (IDE) (Du et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2009

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers have a much increased risk of developing sporadic AD compared to non-carriers.
source: Whatever the precise mechanism, APOE-ɛ4 carriers have a much increased risk of developing sporadic AD (Corder et al., 1993), of progression to AD if diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (Petersen, 1995), and to develop AD at an earlier age (Corder et al., 1993; van der Flier et al., 2011) compared to non-carriers.
evidence: Supported by citations to Corder et al., 1993

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) have increased risk of progression to AD.
source: Whatever the precise mechanism, APOE-ɛ4 carriers have a much increased risk of developing sporadic AD (Corder et al., 1993), of progression to AD if diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (Petersen, 1995), and to develop AD at an earlier age (Corder et al., 1993; van der Flier et al., 2011) compared to non-carriers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Petersen, 1995

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers develop AD at an earlier age compared to non-carriers.
source: Whatever the precise mechanism, APOE-ɛ4 carriers have a much increased risk of developing sporadic AD (Corder et al., 1993), of progression to AD if diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (Petersen, 1995), and to develop AD at an earlier age (Corder et al., 1993; van der Flier et al., 2011) compared to non-carriers.
evidence: Supported by citations to Corder et al., 1993 and van der Flier et al., 2011

claim: Within groups of AD patients and elderly controls, APOE-ɛ4 carriers show alterations in brain structure and function that follow similar patterns to those that characterise AD, but are stronger than in non-carriers.
source: Within groups of AD patients and elderly controls, APOE-ɛ4 carriers show alterations in brain structure and function that follow similar patterns to those that characterise AD, but are stronger than in non-carriers.
evidence: Based on inference from the literature discussed in the introduction

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers present with more severely atrophied temporal areas.
source: Imaging studies show that APOE-ɛ4 carriers present with more severely atrophied temporal areas (Filippini et al., 2009a; Filippini et al., 2009b; Juottonen et al., 1998), and have elevated levels in temporo-parietal areas of the two main harmful brain deposits seen in AD: the tau protein (Ossenkoppele et al., 2016), causing neurofibrillary tangles, and amyloid-β (Drzezga et al., 2009), the peptide accumulating in the pathognomonic intercellular plaques.
evidence: Supported by citations to Filippini et al., 2009a; Filippini et al., 2009b; Juottonen et al., 1998

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers have elevated levels of tau protein in temporo-parietal areas.
source: Imaging studies show that APOE-ɛ4 carriers present with more severely atrophied temporal areas (Filippini et al., 2009a; Filippini et al., 2009b; Juottonen et al., 1998), and have elevated levels in temporo-parietal areas of the two main harmful brain deposits seen in AD: the tau protein (Ossenkoppele et al., 2016), causing neurofibrillary tangles, and amyloid-β (Drzezga et al., 2009), the peptide accumulating in the pathognomonic intercellular plaques.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ossenkoppele et al., 2016

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers have elevated levels of amyloid-β in temporo-parietal areas.
source: Imaging studies show that APOE-ɛ4 carriers present with more severely atrophied temporal areas (Filippini et al., 2009a; Filippini et al., 2009b; Juottonen et al., 1998), and have elevated levels in temporo-parietal areas of the two main harmful brain deposits seen in AD: the tau protein (Ossenkoppele et al., 2016), causing neurofibrillary tangles, and amyloid-β (Drzezga et al., 2009), the peptide accumulating in the pathognomonic intercellular plaques.
evidence: Supported by citation to Drzezga et al., 2009

claim: Neural oscillations, particularly in frequency bands such as the alpha band, have been linked to patterns of white matter connectivity.
source: These neural oscillations, particularly in frequency bands such as the alpha band, have been linked to patterns of white matter connectivity (Teipel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teipel et al., 2009

claim: APOE plays a role in lipid transport, important for myelination of white matter.
source: APOE plays a role in lipid transport, important for myelination of white matter (Herrup, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herrup, 2015

claim: M/EEG studies in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown changes in the oscillatory alpha band.
source: To date, M/EEG studies in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown changes in the oscillatory alpha band (Babiloni et al., 2006; Canuet et al., 2012; de Waal et al., 2013; Jelic et al., 1997; Kramer et al., 2008; Ponomareva et al., 2008) and in the much lower-frequency delta band (Cuesta et al., 2015; de Waal et al., 2013) in regions similar to those reduced in AD and MCI.
evidence: Supported by citations to Babiloni et al., 2006; Canuet et al., 2012; de Waal et al., 2013; Jelic et al., 1997; Kramer et al., 2008; Ponomareva et al., 2008

claim: M/EEG studies in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown changes in the delta band.
source: To date, M/EEG studies in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown changes in the oscillatory alpha band (Babiloni et al., 2006; Canuet et al., 2012; de Waal et al., 2013; Jelic et al., 1997; Kramer et al., 2008; Ponomareva et al., 2008) and in the much lower-frequency delta band (Cuesta et al., 2015; de Waal et al., 2013) in regions similar to those reduced in AD and MCI.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cuesta et al., 2015; de Waal et al., 2013

claim: One small-sample MEG study found that low-frequency (theta) oscillations were increased in the medial frontal cortex of young APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: One very small-sample study has measured MEG oscillations in healthy young genotyped individuals, and found that low-frequency (theta) oscillations were increased in the medial frontal cortex of APOE-ɛ4 carriers, but did not investigate the alpha band, nor connectivity between brain regions (Filbey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Filbey et al., 2006

claim: The study included 51 APOE-ɛ4 carriers and 108 non-carriers in the young cohort.
source: Of the 183 participants, 51 participants were identified as heterozygote or homozygote APOE-ɛ4 carriers, and 108 as not carrying an ɛ4 allele (demographic details in Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated participant numbers from the study

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers did not significantly differ from non-carriers in age, gender, years of education, hippocampal volume, head motion during recording, or number of good-quality resting-state data epochs.
source: APOE-ɛ4 carriers did not significantly differ from non-carriers in age, gender, years of education, hippocampal volume, head motion during the recording or number of good-quality resting-state data epochs included in the analysis (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons reported in Table 1

claim: APOE-ɛ4 carriers performed better than non-carriers on the NAB Mazes task (reasoning and problem solving) with p=0.03.
source: Performance differed on only 1 out of 8 cognitive tasks, the NAB Mazes task (reasoning and problem solving), where ɛ4 carriers performed better than non-carriers, but this result (p=0.03) did not survive a false-discovery-rate correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from cognitive task performance

claim: The NAB Mazes task performance difference did not survive false-discovery-rate correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Performance differed on only 1 out of 8 cognitive tasks, the NAB Mazes task (reasoning and problem solving), where ɛ4 carriers performed better than non-carriers, but this result (p=0.03) did not survive a false-discovery-rate correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001).
evidence: Supported by statistical correction procedure

claim: There was no significant difference in cortical thickness, volume, or area in any region of the Desikan-Killiany atlas between APOE-ɛ4 carriers and non-carriers when corrected for multiple comparisons.
source: Similarly, within the 68 regions of the Desikan-Killiany gyral-based atlas, there was no significant difference found in cortical thickness, volume or area, in any region, when corrected for multiple comparisons.
evidence: Supported by structural MRI analysis results

claim: The beta band has the greatest number of valid connections (224) among individual frequency bands in the APOE-ɛ4 analysis.
source: In the top row, it is clearly evident that, for the individual frequency bands, the beta band has the greatest number of valid connections (224) and the highest number of edges (n = 13) that exceed our initial thresholding criterion of p<0.05 (uncorrected).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: All edges showing significant differences in the beta band show increased connectivity in APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: In the top row, it is clearly evident that, for the individual frequency bands, the beta band has the greatest number of valid connections (224) and the highest number of edges (n = 13) that exceed our initial thresholding criterion of p<0.05 (uncorrected). All of these edges show increased connectivity in the beta band.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: The Combined maps show more edges (n = 282) than any individual frequency band.
source: In the Combined maps, there are not only more edges than any of the individual bands (n = 282) but this synthesised vector combination also shows enhanced sensitivity to cohort effects, with more connections found to be significantly different at the edge-level (n = 31), the cluster-size level (n = 19) and after cohort resampling tests (n = 26).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: The Combined maps show enhanced sensitivity to cohort effects with 31 connections significantly different at the edge-level.
source: In the Combined maps, there are not only more edges than any of the individual bands (n = 282) but this synthesised vector combination also shows enhanced sensitivity to cohort effects, with more connections found to be significantly different at the edge-level (n = 31), the cluster-size level (n = 19) and after cohort resampling tests (n = 26).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is evidence of hypoconnectivity in left medial temporal regions, including the hippocampus, in APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: Again, the balance of the sign of the effect is skewed towards hyperconnectivity in the majority of comparisons, although, interestingly, there is some evidence of hypoconnectivity (blue lines) in left medial temporal regions, including the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is a bias towards effects in the right hemisphere in APOE-ɛ4 carriers, with many significantly different edges arising from the right parietal cortex.
source: What can also be observed is a bias towards effects in the right hemisphere, with many of the significantly different edges arising from the right parietal cortex, but also including medial precuneus regions.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: Connectivity differences in APOE-ɛ4 carriers at least partially overlap with posterior regions of the human default-mode network (DMN).
source: These differences therefore at least partially overlap with posterior regions of the human default-mode network (DMN).
evidence: Based on inference from the spatial pattern of effects

claim: The only differences in oscillatory activity found using TFCE (p<0.05 corrected) were in the two gamma ranges, 40–60 Hz and 60–140 Hz.
source: When we assessed activity across the brain using a voxelwise assessment of temporal variability in the amplitude envelope at each location in the brain, the only differences found using TFCE (p<0.05 corrected) were in the two gamma ranges, 40–60 Hz and 60–140 Hz and are shown in Figure 2.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Gamma hyperactivities in APOE-ɛ4 carriers were exclusively in a right-lateralised profile, distributed over lateral parietal, temporal and frontal regions.
source: These were exclusively gamma hyperactivities in a right-lateralised profile, distributed over lateral parietal, temporal and frontal regions.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: When a more conservative voxel-level threshold (p<0.05, corrected) was applied, only one region survived in the 60–140 Hz range, localised over the right middle and inferior frontal gyri.
source: When a more conservative voxel-level threshold (p<0.05, corrected) was applied, only one region survived in the 60–140 Hz range, localised over the right middle and inferior frontal gyri.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: AD patients compared to age-matched controls show strongly decreased oscillatory connectivity in predominantly parieto-temporal connections.
source: In our reanalysis of a subset of the same dataset, using the current pipeline (Figure 3) to compare AD patients to age-matched controls, we show strongly decreased oscillatory connectivity in predominantly parieto-temporal connections, with the most significant, and extensive, effects visible in the Alpha and Beta ranges.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: The most significant and extensive connectivity effects in AD patients are visible in the Alpha and Beta ranges.
source: In our reanalysis of a subset of the same dataset, using the current pipeline (Figure 3) to compare AD patients to age-matched controls, we show strongly decreased oscillatory connectivity in predominantly parieto-temporal connections, with the most significant, and extensive, effects visible in the Alpha and Beta ranges.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: In contrast to the APOE-ɛ4 analysis, most of the observed significant cohort differences in AD are reduced connectivity (hypoconnectivity).
source: We also note that, in contrast to the APOE-ɛ4 analysis, most of the observed significant cohort differences are reduced connectivity, i.e. hypoconnectivity, in AD compared to elderly controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: The AD cohort of patients did not show any significant differences in oscillatory envelope temporal standard-deviation at any AAL node, in any frequency band, compared to age-matched controls.
source: Finally, when using the temporal standard-deviation of the oscillatory envelope to quantify activation at each AAL node, this cohort of patients did not show any significant differences, in any frequency band, compared to their age-matched controls.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of AD patient data

claim: In the Alpha band there is a single occipital connection (Cuneus left to Lingual left) that has reduced connectivity in both APOE-ɛ4 carriers and AD.
source: In the Alpha band there is a single occipital connection that has reduced connectivity in both APOE-ɛ4 carriers and AD.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: In the Beta band there is a single connection from the medial precuneus region to right lateral parietal that shows hyperconnectivity in APOE-ɛ4 carriers and hypoconnectivity in people with AD.
source: In the Beta band there is a single connection from the medial precuneus region to right lateral parietal that shows hyperconnectivity in APOE-ɛ4 carriers and hypoconnectivity in people with AD, compared to their respective controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: In the Combined analysis, there are three connections in the right lateral-parietal/temporal region that show hyperconnectivity in APOE-ɛ4 carriers and hypoconnectivity in AD.
source: Similarly, in the Combined analysis, there are three connections in the right lateral-parietal/temporal region that show this same pattern of effects.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 2

claim: Using pooled classification based on valid edges in all frequency ranges, the classifier was able to distinguish AD patients from elderly controls with an AUC of 77.6% (p<0.02).
source: Using pooled classification, based on valid edges in all frequency ranges, the classifier was, on average, able to distinguish AD patients from elderly controls with reasonable specificity and sensitivity and a significant AUC of 77.6% (p<0.02).
evidence: Supported by machine learning classification results shown in Table 3

claim: Performance classifying APOE-ɛ4 carriers from non-carriers was significantly above chance level with an AUC of 63.5% (p<0.005).
source: Performance classifying APOE-ɛ4 carriers from non-carriers was also significantly above the chance level of 50%, with an AUC of 63.5% (p<0.005).
evidence: Supported by machine learning classification results shown in Table 3

claim: When a classifier trained to distinguish APOE-ɛ4 carriers was used to predict AD cases from controls, performance was significantly below chance with an AUC of 31.8%.
source: Interestingly, when we trained a classifier to distinguish APOE-ɛ4 carriers, using all data from the young cohort, and then predict AD cases from controls, performance was significantly below chance, with an AUC of 31.8%.
evidence: Supported by machine learning classification results shown in Table 3

claim: The reversed labelling in the cross-experiment classification was equivalent to an AUC of 68.2% that is above chance but only a trend to significance (p<0.14).
source: If we assume that the classifier is predicting reverse labelling in the disease group, this was equivalent to an AUC of 68.2% that is above chance, but only a trend to significance (p<0.14).
evidence: Supported by machine learning classification results shown in Table 3

claim: The results suggest that the right parietal cortex is a particularly important area in the risk for, and development of, AD.
source: Our results therefore suggest that the right parietal cortex is a particularly important area in the risk for, and development of, AD.
evidence: Based on inference from the spatial pattern of connectivity and activity effects

claim: An initial hyperconnectivity/hyperactivity centred around right parietal cortex may have a cascade of effects that lead to eventual disconnection in AD.
source: Although our study can only show an implied association between early hyperconnectivity and later hypoconnectivity, we could speculate that an initial hyperconnectivity/hyperactivity centred around (right) parietal cortex has a cascade of effects that may lead to eventual disconnection in AD.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed patterns

claim: The hyperconnectivity effect is initially right-dominant but may spread over time to more widespread effects across the cortex and hemispheres.
source: Although initially a right-dominant effect, this may spread over time to more widespread effects across the cortex and hemispheres.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about temporal progression

claim: Gamma band oscillations mostly reflect local, rather than global processing, whilst alpha/beta underpin longer-range interactions.
source: This result is consistent with theories suggesting that gamma band oscillations mostly reflecting local, rather than global processing, whilst alpha/beta underpin longer-range interactions (Donner and Siegel, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donner and Siegel, 2011

claim: A realistically-coupled set of local gamma oscillators at multiple simulated brain regions led to long-range, slowly varying, coupled amplitude-envelopes in the alpha/beta range.
source: Our results are also consistent with a recent computational model in which it was shown that a realistically-coupled set of local gamma oscillators, at multiple simulated brain regions, led to long-range, slowly varying, coupled amplitude-envelopes, but in the alpha/beta range (Cabral et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cabral et al., 2014

claim: Higher-gamma band activity (60–140 Hz) may be correlated with neuronal spiking rates.
source: Finally, it has been suggested that higher-gamma band activity, such as our 60–140 Hz band, may be correlated with neuronal spiking rates (Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray and Maunsell, 2011

claim: The higher gamma-band activity seen in APOE-ɛ4 carriers may be a reflection of neuronal hyperactivity associated with increased amyloid-β seen in rodent AD models.
source: If true then the higher gamma-band activity we see in APOE-ɛ4 carriers may be a reflection of the neuronal hyperactivity, associated with increased amyloid-β, seen in rodent AD models (Stargardt et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citation to Stargardt et al., 2015

claim: MEG studies using Graph Theory network measures have identified a loss of connectivity in AD, with the parietal cortex as the most affected hub.
source: MEG studies using Graph Theory network measures have also identified a loss of connectivity in AD, with the parietal cortex as the most affected hub (de Haan et al., 2012b; Tijms et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Haan et al., 2012b; Tijms et al., 2013

claim: Beta band oscillations are thought to play an important role in long-range functional connectivity.
source: Effects were found specifically in the beta band – thought to play an important role in long-range functional connectivity (Schnitzler and Gross, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schnitzler and Gross, 2005

claim: Cuesta et al. found that elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers showed differences only in the delta frequency band (1–4 Hz), focused around a frontal brain hub.
source: Using the higher spatial resolution of MEG, Cuesta et al. (Cuesta et al., 2015) studied source-localised connectivity in elderly participants with and without MCI, and found that APOE-ɛ4 carriers showed differences only in a much lower frequency band than alpha (delta, 1–4 Hz), focused around a frontal brain hub.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cuesta et al., 2015

claim: One small MEG study (N = 8) found increases in mainly medial-frontal theta-band (3.5–7 Hz) oscillatory power during a working memory task in young APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: To our knowledge, only one small MEG study (N = 8) has previously investigated young APOE-ɛ4 carriers, and found increases in mainly medial-frontal theta-band (3.5–7 Hz) oscillatory power during a working memory task (Filbey et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Filbey et al., 2006

claim: The blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response within the default-mode network (DMN) is reduced in healthy ageing.
source: Functional MRI (fMRI) resting-state studies typically show that the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response within the default-mode network (DMN) is reduced in healthy ageing (Damoiseaux et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damoiseaux et al., 2008

claim: The reduction in DMN BOLD response is accelerated in AD.
source: This reduction is accelerated in AD (Buckner et al., 2008) and is also modified in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers compared to non-carriers (Sheline et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buckner et al., 2008

claim: DMN BOLD response is modified in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers compared to non-carriers.
source: This reduction is accelerated in AD (Buckner et al., 2008) and is also modified in elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers compared to non-carriers (Sheline et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheline et al., 2010

claim: Filippini et al. found increased co-activation of areas within the DMN for young APOE-ɛ4 carriers, focused on hippocampal and frontal regions.
source: Filippini et al. (Filippini et al., 2009a) previously investigated DMN BOLD activity in a small sample of young APOE-ɛ4 carriers versus non-carriers (N = 18 each) using an independent component analysis (ICA) technique. They found increased co-activation of areas within the DMN for ɛ4 carriers, which were focused on hippocampal and frontal, but posterior regions were not significantly different.
evidence: Supported by citation to Filippini et al., 2009a

claim: Filippini et al. found an increase in the sensorimotor network in young APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: Furthermore, they also found an increase in the sensorimotor network.
evidence: Supported by citation to Filippini et al., 2009a (implied from context)

claim: Westlye et al. found significant increases in network activity for older healthy APOE-ɛ4 carriers in posterior regions of the DMN, including the precuneus and lateral parietal regions as well as frontal cortex.
source: In a more recent resting state-fMRI study of older, but healthy, APOE-ɛ4 carriers it was found that, as well as replicating Fillipini et al.'s finding of increased hippocampal DMN connectivity, significant increases in network activity were also found for APOE-ɛ4 carriers in posterior regions of the DMN, including the precuneus, and lateral parietal regions as well as frontal cortex (Westlye et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Westlye et al., 2011

claim: Westlye et al. found that frontal and posterior-lateral regions were only significantly increased in the right hemisphere in APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: Importantly, these frontal and posterior-lateral regions were only significantly increased in the right hemisphere (their Figure 1D and Table 3), showing good concordance with our findings of oscillatory hyperconnectivity in similar right-hemisphere regions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Westlye et al., 2011

claim: Some recent task-based fMRI studies have shown APOE-ɛ4 carrier hyperactivity in posterior parts of the DMN.
source: Finally, we note that some recent task-based fMRI studies have also shown APOE-ɛ4 carrier hyperactivity in posterior parts of the DMN (Hodgetts et al., 2019; Shine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hodgetts et al., 2019; Shine et al., 2015

claim: Hyperactivity/hyperconnectivity of the DMN in young APOE-ɛ4 carriers may reflect reduced network efficiency/flexibility.
source: Interestingly, the authors of these studies speculate that hyperactivity/hyperconnectivity of the DMN in these young APOE-ɛ4 carriers may reflect reduced network efficiency/flexibility.
evidence: Speculative reasoning cited from other studies

claim: There is little or no evidence of cortical volume changes, including hypothesised hippocampal volume decreases, in young APOE-ɛ4 carriers.
source: Note that in our cohort, and other previous studies, there is little or no evidence of cortical volume changes, including hypothesised hippocampal volume decreases (Filippini et al., 2009a; Heise et al., 2011; O'Dwyer et al., 2012; Wishart et al., 2006), suggesting that changes in both haemodynamic and oscillatory brain function can be detected before changes in brain structure in the pathway of increased risk for AD (Figure 5, lower panel, (Hampel et al., 2011)).
evidence: Supported by citations to Filippini et al., 2009a; Heise et al., 2011; O'Dwyer et al., 2012; Wishart et al., 2006

claim: Changes in both haemodynamic and oscillatory brain function can be detected before changes in brain structure in the pathway of increased risk for AD.
source: Note that in our cohort, and other previous studies, there is little or no evidence of cortical volume changes, including hypothesised hippocampal volume decreases (Filippini et al., 2009a; Heise et al., 2011; O'Dwyer et al., 2012; Wishart et al., 2006), suggesting that changes in both haemodynamic and oscillatory brain function can be detected before changes in brain structure in the pathway of increased risk for AD (Figure 5, lower panel, (Hampel et al., 2011)).
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of structural changes and presence of functional changes

claim: Increased amyloid-β is related to increased neural activity in rodent disease models during Braak pre-symptomatic stages 0, I and II.
source: For example, it was shown in a rodent disease model that during Braak pre-symptomatic stages 0, I and II, amyloid-β starts to accumulate within neurons, whilst at the same time synaptic activity rises within the neurons (i.e. hyperactivity).
evidence: Based on inference from rodent studies

claim: As the disease progresses to Braak stage VI and amyloid-β causes plaques, synaptic activity falls (hypoactivity).
source: As the disease progresses to Braak stage VI, and amyloid-β becomes significant enough to cause plaques, synaptic activity then falls (i.e. hypoactivity).
evidence: Based on inference from rodent studies

claim: The rise in amyloid-β appeared to be linked to a reduction of activity in the Insulin-Degrading Enzyme (IDE) in rodent models.
source: Interestingly, it appeared that the rise in amyloid-β appeared to be linked to a reduction of activity in the Insulin-Degrading Enzyme (IDE).
evidence: Based on inference from rodent studies

claim: Carrying the APOE-ɛ4 allele leads to impaired myelination, mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced cholinergic function and vascular pathology.
source: Experimental studies have demonstrated that carrying the APOE-ɛ4 allele leads to a wide range of effects in the brain, including impaired myelination, mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced cholinergic function and vascular pathology (Reinvang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinvang et al., 2013

claim: Healthy elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers show increased uptake of amyloid-binding PET ligands (PiB).
source: Healthy elderly APOE-ɛ4 carriers also show increased uptake of amyloid-binding PET ligands (PiB) (Morris et al., 2010; Reiman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morris et al., 2010; Reiman et al., 2009

claim: Post-mortem studies of middle-aged APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown an increase in senile amyloid-β plaques, with some evidence at ages as young as 30.
source: Already in middle age, post-mortem studies of APOE-ɛ4 carriers have shown an increase in senile amyloid-β plaques (Kok et al., 2009), with some evidence of this even at ages as young as 30.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kok et al., 2009

claim: APOE-ɛ4 leads to reduced levels of insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE), one of the most important enzymes for amyloid-β clearance.
source: For example, one study has shown that APOE-ɛ4 leads to reduced levels of insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE), one of the most important enzymes for amyloid-β clearance (Du et al., 2009) and, as described above, is reduced during pre-symptomatic stages in rodent disease models which also show synaptic hyperactivity (Stargardt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2009

claim: Neural hyperactivity can occur in APOE-ɛ4 mouse models in the absence of overt amyloid or tau pathology via a mechanism in which APOE-ɛ4 leads to an overall decrease in inhibition.
source: It has also been shown in a recent study, however, that neural hyperactivity can also occur in APOE-ɛ4 mouse models in the absence of overt amyloid or tau pathology (Nuriel et al., 2017) via a mechanism in which APOE-ɛ4 leads to an overall decrease in inhibition caused by a reduced responsiveness of excitatory neurons to GABAergic input.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nuriel et al., 2017

claim: APOE-ɛ4 related shift in the excitation/inhibition balance leads to hyperactivity that later results in increased amyloid deposition and increased risk of AD.
source: The authors therefore suggest that it is this APOE-ɛ4 related shift in the excitation/inhibition balance that leads to hyperactivity that later results in increased amyloid deposition, and hence increased risk of AD.
evidence: Speculative reasoning cited from Nuriel et al., 2017

claim: Increased amyloid-β is not sufficient to cause AD.
source: It is important to note, though, that increased amyloid-β is not sufficient to cause AD (Herrup, 2015; Sheline et al., 2010) and the presence of APOE-ɛ4 does not guarantee progression to AD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrup, 2015; Sheline et al., 2010

claim: Areas predisposed to hyperconnectivity are thought to be prone to yield increased accumulation of amyloid-β.
source: Our findings therefore support theories based on rodent models (Stargardt et al., 2015), human computational models (de Haan et al., 2012b) and MCI data (Maestú et al., 2015) that propose that hyperactivity, ultimately related to hyperconnectivity, may be at the heart of brain dysfunction that could eventually lead to AD, and provides compelling evidence that this may already happen in early adulthood. Areas predisposed to hyperconnectivity are thought to be prone to yield increased accumulation of amyloid-β (Myers et al., 2014), supported by longitudinal PET and fMRI studies which found that hippocampal hyperactivation in elderly individuals leads to widespread increased deposition of amyloid-β as well as hippocampal signal loss and memory decline, although these studies found no effect of APOE-ɛ4 (O'Brien et al., 2010) or there was insufficient power to test this (Leal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Myers et al., 2014

evidence: Supported by citations to O'Brien et al., 2010 and Leal et al., 2017

claim: The exploratory analysis combining connectivity maps from different frequency bands using a vector sum approach revealed more robust connectivity patterns across participants with increased number of valid edge connections.
